items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: So he and I were good friends.

ctx.x: Yeah, the Reno Club. They all went back to join Basie. And about that time, Lucky Millinder sent a telegram to some trumpet player there in St. Louis he wanted to come but he sent tickets to a friend of mine who was playing with the St. Louis Crackerjacks. I met him with then, named Harold Arnold, he was a tenor player. So he and I were good friends. So he said, 'Well, I got a ticket here so I have to get the trumpet player Lucky sent for.' So he said, 'Why don't you take the ticket and let's both go to New York.
So I said, "Well, he didn't send for me, he sent for somebody else." So he said, "What difference does it make," you know. So, okay, we got on the train and went to New York.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And I knew Harold Arnold who enticed me to go to New York on this fake ticket under somebody else’s

ctx.x: How did you fit in as a youngster, this was your first real name band, how did you fit in with Lucky’s band?
Naturally, they had a boy in there from St. Louis, Tab Smith, I knew him. And I knew Harold Arnold who enticed me to go to New York on this fake ticket under somebody else’s

name. But I was still scared of Lucky, the way he would talk. He didn’t know anything about music, one note from the other, but he was a great director. He would hear something arranged one time, he would know where he wanted the dynamics put. As you followed him, it was a beautiful show.
